summary: A revised specification of the Mail Transfer Protocol, an early protocol for delivering mail between hosts. It was itself superseded by the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Replaced by RFC 788.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 780 specifies MTP, a protocol for transferring mail between hosts and relaying it across transport environments. It also defines two optional schemes for sending one message to multiple recipients; RFC 788 later obsoleted this version.

subtitle: A mail transfer protocol with relaying and two optional multi-recipient schemes.

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a protocol for transferring mail reliably across transport environments, including cases where an intermediate host must relay it.
tldr.mechanism: MTP uses a sender and receiver exchanging commands and replies over a reliable ordered stream; a MAIL command carries sender and receiver paths, followed by message text.

facts.label: Message text terminator
facts.value: A line containing only a period

sections.title: Sender, Receiver, and Relay Hosts
sections.content:
MTP requires a reliable, ordered data stream but is independent of the particular transport subsystem. A sender-MTP establishes a full-duplex channel to a receiver-MTP. The receiver may be the destination or an intermediate server that relays the message into another transport environment.

A MAIL command carries a sender path and a receiver path. The receiver path can list hosts for source routing, while the sender path provides a return route for delivery problems.
sections.plainLanguage: One MTP process sends commands and mail to another, which replies. If the recipient is on another transport system, an intermediate MTP host can relay the message.

sections.title: Sending and Relaying Mail
sections.content:
For basic mail, the receiver accepts the MAIL command and returns a 354 reply to begin message input. The sender transmits the text and ends it with a line containing only a period; the receiver then returns a completion reply. A transparency rule lets the sender transmit a text line that begins with a period without ending the message accidentally.

When relaying, each MTP removes its own name from the receiver path and places it at the beginning of the sender path. This preserves a route toward the originator if delivery later fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender supplies the message after the receiver agrees to accept it. A line containing only a period ends the text, and each relay updates the forward and return paths.

sections.title: Sending One Message to Several Recipients
sections.content:
MTP defines two optional multi-recipient schemes. In recipients-first mode, the sender names and receives a response for each recipient before sending the text. In text-first mode, the sender sends the text first and then specifies recipients individually. The sender can ask which scheme the receiver prefers, but the receiver chooses which scheme is used.

The schemes are optional. They allow one copy of the message text to be sent for multiple recipients, while enabling a receiver to report recipient-specific results in text-first mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver chooses whether recipients are listed before or after the message text. Either scheme lets the sender reuse one message for multiple recipients.

sections.title: Replies and Minimum Commands
sections.content:
Every command generates exactly one reply. A reply has a three-digit code followed by text; programs use the code to determine what to do next, while the text is intended for people. The first digit distinguishes preliminary, successful, intermediate, temporary negative, and permanent negative replies.

The minimum receiver implementation must support MAIL, QUIT, and NOOP. When using TCP, the appendix assigns MTP service port 57. RFC 780 was later obsoleted by RFC 788.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command gets one reply, and its three-digit code tells the sender whether to continue, retry, or stop. The memo specifies a small minimum set of commands.
